utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber had in mind to examine one of the witnesses called by the Chamber, but our latest information is that the witness the Chamber called has not arrived. I take it that the parties were informed over the weekend on late -- the last attempts to get in touch with the witness. There was an e-mail from --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we weren't, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But we took -- we simply took no news as no news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it didn't cause us any problems. No -- but we received an e-mail this morning, Your Honour. I've just been told in the last few minutes of an e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. I -- that was the situation for us as well. I took some pro-active steps to contact VWU at the last minute and found out that the situation was as we understood it to be throughout. But as I don't anticipate that the situation will necessarily arise again, but perhaps as suggested by Mr. Stewart, impliedly, it would be helpful if we were notified by VWS of the circumstances to the best of their knowledge at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My information was that the last attempt to get in telephone contact with that witness, that although the telephone was answered by a male person, that the report was that the witness was not there. The Chamber -- because until now of course everything was -- we have dealt with the matter in private session. At this moment the Chamber wants to deal with the matter in open session. Because this Chamber, after having heard witnesses called by the parties, has decided to call some Chamber witnesses pursuant to Rule 98 of the Rules. And the first of those witnesses is Branko Djeric, Prime Minister of Republika Srpska during the indictment period. The Chamber has attempted on various occasions to get in contact with Professor Djeric, first by phone, then through mail. And Mr. Djeric was either not available or refused any contact with the Chamber. Finally, the Chamber issued a subpoena ad testificandum, which was to be served on him by the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Chamber was notified that Professor Djeric refused to receive the subpoena, despite being orally notified by the state official that this might cause the Chamber to start contempt proceedings against him, pursuant to Rule 77 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Chamber hereby verifies that Professor Djeric in fact did not appear at the scheduled time and place and therefore has not met with what he was asked to do in the -- or he was ordered to do in the subpoena. The Chamber will now consider what measures it will take. But meanwhile, the Chamber hereby lifts all confidentiality of the following documents relating to calling Professor Branko Djeric as a Chamber witness: That is the letter that was sent to him on the 17th of May; that is the subpoena ad testificandum, dated the 8th of June; and the report by the state official filed on the 20th of June. That's as far as the Chamber witness is concerned, Mr. Djeric. Any matter to be raised in this respect by either Defence or Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll try to use our time this morning in dealing with housekeeping and procedural matters. But before I do so, I was informed that the registry received this morning material from Mr. Krajisnik. Of course we are now in a different stage. Mr. Krajisnik, you are not a witness anymore who brings material that he considers to be relevant, but you are now again the accused, who should first consult with counsel before -- before delivering documents to -- to the Chamber. I don't know whether you'd discussed this material with counsel. If not, I'll return it to you so you have an opportunity to do so. If you have discussed the material with counsel, then of course I would like to hear why this un-Orthodox way of introducing this material was chosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say we would be very grateful. We have not had the opportunity. We would be extremely grateful if Your Honour would do exactly what is suggested. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, you have the other material, everything to be given back to -- yes, Mr. Krajisnik. You would like to say something about it? If so, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with your conclusion, but I would like to inform you about something. It has to do with the Bileca case and the tape that the Court personnel should have listened to. I listened to it and I made a transcript, and on the basis of that you will see that what the Prosecution said is not correct. I agree that I can talk about this to Mr. Stewart, too. So the transcript is incorrect. I have video footage here as well, and you've got the CD, too. And I've provided other arguments as well, supporting what I said. That is why I agree that I should discuss this with Mr. Stewart, but everything that I have provided you with is correct. Thank you very much. And sorry for having taken the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just add that we -- on Friday Mr. Krajisnik and I and Mr. Josse agreed that we would discuss this at the UNDU today. We -- everybody in court has the same interest in getting through today's business as soon as possible. From our point of view as soon as we are through our business in court, we will then be able to go and see Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll try and go through the pending issues and the housekeeping matters as soon as possible. I take it if the material Mr. Krajisnik sheds any new light on matters if you want to introduce that, the Prosecution will be informed about that at earliest possibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the parties have received an agenda, and I will go through the items one by one, but the first one -- any problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does the Court recall or can the registrar assist us in when the agenda was assisted. We're not aware of having one at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I do understand from our Legal Officer that it was mailed to you on Friday, sent by e-mail Friday. It's, of course, a very practical document. It's no --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For what it's worth, we've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've got it? Do we have another copy so that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the message was sent on the 23rd of June and was addressed, apart from others, also to Mr. Tieger, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Wijermars. It was sent at 3.56 p.m. I hope that this will not -- well, most of the issues of course are not new because they are pending. Let's go through it. The first one on the agenda is the decision on acts and exemplars related to an exhibit P340. I would rather delay that for a while. The Chamber is thought it could give an oral decision right away, but might take a couple of hours or even half a day more time. Then the second item on the agenda is P1072. The issue here is whether this document, which is a declaration on ethnic distribution of selected names in BiH, population census 31st of March, 1991, a document dated the 26th of January, 2006, whether there would be any objection to have this document admitted without a B/C/S translation. It's mainly a list, names, numbers, rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then when there's no objection to this format without a translation in B/C/S, the Chamber admits P1072 into evidence. Next on the agenda, P1177A and P1177B, Nielsen source material. It has been renumbered, but there's no formal decision yet that they are admitted into evidence. That decision is now delivered, so these two items are now in evidence. Next item on the agenda is P1148, which is Karadzic notebook. Only limited portions of P1148 have been the subject of examination. I'm thinking Mr. Kecmanovic, 4th of April, 2006. The Prosecution has tendered the whole of the notebook, and the Defence can make submissions so that we can render a decision on admission after that. Mr. Josse. I notice, by the way, that it was mainly pages 7, 8, and 9 that were subject of questioning, and it was during the cross-examination of Mr. Kecmanovic on the date I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have two observations in relation to this, and interestingly our arguments are, to some extent, foreshadowed in what was said when the admission of this document was last discussed in this Chamber at page 22560 of the transcript. Mr. Tieger very frankly said: "The fact that we didn't refer to it repeatedly during the course of the cross-examination is only an unfortunate reflection of an attempt to meet the time constraints." And let me immediately say, Your Honour, that of course the Defence accept that. But the position has become clearer in that regard because the Prosecution did not use it in the course of their cross-examination of Mr. Krajisnik. And I dare say, my learned friend will say the reason for that is time constraints yet again. Nonetheless, it hasn't been used, and Mr. Krajisnik therefore has not had an opportunity to deal with it, and it hasn't featured further in the evidence in this case, save the pages Your Honour has referred to so far as Mr. Kecmanovic is concerned. Our second point is really the issue that Your Honour mentioned to the parties immediately after the comments of Mr. Tieger that I have just alluded to. Your Honour said: "First of all, for your information, this Chamber does not start at 7.15, once we are out of this courtroom, to start immediately to read the whole of the notebooks. And until now we have focussed on the portions that were presented to us. We have quite a lot of things to do." And then Your Honour, with respect, very sensibly goes on and suggests: Let's wait and see and wait whether the notebook is further used in evidence. Our concern is this: We are unclear as to what role, if any, this notebook would play in this case if the whole of it is admitted into evidence. Will it be the case that the Chamber would go away and read it from start to finish and then consider it as part of the evidence in this case as a whole? Or would it be that the Chamber would wait and see whether the parties refer to it in the course of their final briefs and/or closing arguments? Any guidance in that regard would be most helpful because, Your Honour, we submit that realistically, unless the Chamber is going to say: Well, it will be read from cover to cover if it's admitted into evidence, then the safest and proper course is to leave things exactly as they are at the moment and only admit into evidence those parts that have been referred to during the cross-examination of Mr. Kecmanovic. So our position is that we seek -- we invite the Chamber to rule that only those parts that were put to the witness should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Two things preliminarily. First, it's important to be clear on what this document is. It's been referred to as the Karadzic notebook, but what in fact is, is an account of the Cutileiro negotiations, a very detailed account akin to a diary or a journal or even virtually a stenographic note-taking at some portions of the discussions that took place between roughly February 27th and March 18th. Now, although I want to limit my analysis of its admissibility to the technical, legal points at issue and not weave it into the general argument about the case, it's a little -- this document became relevant because of the Defence emphasis on the Cutileiro discussions and negotiations. Now here's a document, an SDS document, which purports to be an account of those events which, in some systems one might say paradoxically, the Prosecution seeks to admit for the Court's benefit so it can see what happens during those discussions and the Defence somehow shrinks from. So that's the starting position with this document. I accept, of course, that we were not able to get into a detailed discussion and analysis of every point raised in the document. And to some extent, that may limit the weight which the Court wants to give any single individual excerpt from that diary. On the other hand, when we looked at the diary to see -- or the journal or however we want to label it, to see the extent to which it was corroborated, for example, by accounts in the Bosnian Serb Assembly about what had just transpired in the negotiations, and there was considerable overlaps. So where that overlap occurs, clearly the Court will be benefitted if those points are at issue. To the extent that there may be some point that has never been the subject of any discussion or attention during the course of that case, then the Court might have some reluctance about according it similar weight. But the most significant point is simply this: The Defence has put the Cutileiro discussions in the forefront, for better or worse, of different aspects of this case. Here's a document which bears directly on that, which can be of considerable potential assistance to the Court. As the Defence is aware, on many occasions in the past, we have attempted to resolve any admissibility issues with them under the rubric of an effort to bring as much useful information to the Court on both sides. And I think this document falls squarely in that principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, one question. From the few pages that were dealt with during examination of the witness, it seems that there are also, not only specifically on those questions, just limiting ourselves to the pages. It's, to some extent, also confirms, I would, the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik and confirms even the position of the Defence in some respects, I would say. Therefore -- and again, I emphasise -- I'm just then reading the pages that were 7, 8, and 9 and not any of the others. I do not know whether on any of the others there would be some exculpatory evidence as well. I don't know. But have you considered that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then that's -- thank you. We'll -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just emphasise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're not suggesting that it doesn't contain exculpatory material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But we maintain the stance that I enunciated a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will further consider the matter and we will give a decision. We're not going to do that right away because we didn't know until now what exactly the position of the Defence would be. Then I move on to the next item on the -- next item on the agenda that it's P1258 and P1259, photographic and video evidence of destruction of property. We heard the objections from the Defence on the 12th of June, and we heard some objections and some observations by Mr. Krajisnik on the 21st of June. And I'll now deliver the oral decision. With regard to the CD and photographic material of destruction of property in 1992, the Chamber has heard from the parties and from the accused, the concerns raised have been taken into consideration. The Chamber hereby admits into evidence P1258, the photographic material, and P1259, the CD. The Chamber reiterates the limited purpose of the material, which is to serve as a visualisation of the destruction caused during the conflict. Next item on the agenda is Defence Exhibit D14, that is a news article and a photo from Glas dated 23rd of April, 1992. No English translation has been provided; however, the article was read into the record in full. The first question is whether there are any objections against admission without an English translation, keeping in mind that a translation is on the record as -- well, we find it in the transcript at this moment. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it the Defence would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D14 is admitted into evidence, even without an English translation. And just for the record, I state here that the translation -- that the article was read into the record on pages 2.921 till 2.924, and these are transcript pages. We then move on to the next one, D127, D128. We are waiting, as a matter of fact, for translations into English. When could the Chamber expect to receive the translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm about to say applies to item 7, 8, and 9 on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm deliberately putting it that way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- for obvious reasons. At this precise moment, we are unable to access the TTS. The Chamber may be aware that there have been fairly frequent difficulties with accessing this service, that is a service which enables us to see the progress of translations that have been sent to the CLSS. And therefore, I can't give an answer at this precise moment in relation to any of those items. I am more than content for the Chamber to set some sort of deadline which would allow Mr. Sladojevic to tell the CLSS and would ensure that the matter is reviewed relatively quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These are not very lengthy documents, D127, D128. I mean they are just one or -- well, not any longer than three pages. Because the Chamber would very much like to -- but I'm limiting myself to 7 and 8. The Chamber would like to receive those ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to receive the translations within the next ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know if it's helpful or not, but with respect to item 8 the Court may recall -- those are minutes of a particular session. The Court may recall that the Prosecution obtained and submitted the tape-recording of the -- that actual session. So I don't know if the minutes are still of the same significance to anyone that they would have been before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have to -- it's slipped out of my mind, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Me, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- quite honest. But we'll pay further attention to that, and if that would change a need for a translation, then -- but the tape-recording -- we're talking about a Presidency meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. The minutes were submitted to -- as I recall, to support Mr. Krajisnik's claim -- or at that time Mr. Kecmanovic's claim as -- and then subsequently Mr. Krajisnik's assertion in his testimony, that the Bosnian leadership had at one point considered exchanges or discussed exchanges. And then the issue had not come up subsequently on the agenda. That was apparently reflected in -- although I haven't seen the translation of the minutes, apparently reflected in some way in the minutes. We obtained the actual tape-recording of that session, and during the course of Mr. Krajisnik's cross-examination presented that and it was admitted. So the portions of the Presidency meeting of that date devoted to that issue. So those were available, both in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a look at that and might be so that therefore there would be no need anymore to have that -- have this material translated. We'll look into the matter. Then as far as 9 is concerned, that's a document D171, which is under seal. Here again the question arises whether -- it's a very short document. It has been read into the transcript, so I wonder whether this document could be admitted even without a translation. It has been read into the transcript on transcript pages 22.798 up to 22.800. Here, same procedure as we earlier had. Does the Prosecution object admission without a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We do not, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D171 is admitted into evidence, taking that the Defence has no objections either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have dealt then with agenda item 9. We move on number 10, D174 and D175. These are Bosnian Serb Presidency sessions, 2nd of August, 1992, and 28th of September, 1992. Apart from translation issues, there was also a need to discuss the provenance of the documents with Mr. Krajisnik after he had finished his testimony. Could the Defence inform the Chamber about the present status of those discussions and of translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Translation is as before, same explanation as I gave a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the discussions are concerned, frankly, Your Honour, I had forgotten about this. This agenda was not in existence when we went to the prison on Friday. I do want to specifically discuss this with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You have an opportunity to do so and the Chamber -- these are relatively -- again, relatively short documents, two pages of the 21st Session and four pages of the 32nd Session. If a translation could be provided within the next ten days, that would be highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Agenda item 11, additional documents from D14 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I should have notified the Chamber of this by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is something we haven't forgotten about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are not relying on any of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's then finished. Now we come to a -- not the easiest part. We come to the exhibits tendered by the parties during Mr. Krajisnik's testimony. The parties have received the list from Mr. Haider. I would like to go through it page by page to see whether there are any problematic issues. The list starts at P1180, first page goes up to 1185. Any objections or any problems there?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next page from 1185B up to 1188.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next page, P1188 till P1194.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then on the next page starting with P1195 we find P1197, which is a document that, if admitted, should be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the one I wish to address the Chamber about that one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Court might wish to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it's wise to do so. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The result of what we discussed in private session was that a decision on P1197 will be given, not at this moment but later. Then we'll continue on that same page, P1198 up to P1200.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No other difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No other difficulties. Next page, 1201 up to 1207.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problems there. Then on the next page, starting with 1207.1 we have P1212, which was admitted already, oral decision of the 6th of June, from what I understand, so not something we have to decide on anymore. Anything else on this page which goes up to P1214?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next page starting at P1214.1 goes to P1221 and 1221 has no B/C/S translation yet. Mr. Tieger -- and the same is, by the way, true for the first item on the next page, page 8, P1222 also lacks a B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll have to double-check on that. The review of this material took place in the context of any possible objections, and I'm afraid I just didn't look that the particular box to see whether that issue had been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll hear from you soon. Someone is typing near to a microphone. Then we move on. Anything else on page 8, which goes from P1222 to P1228?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Objection to P1226. The relevant part of the transcript is page 25390. In short, in the context of this document various names were put to Mr. Krajisnik. He readily accepted those names in the context in which they were put to him. No further reference was made to the document. In our submission, the document does not need to be admitted into evidence, and indeed should not be admitted into evidence because it was not further cross-examined upon at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the extent to which a document is cross-examined on is surely not the basis for its admissibility. The subject at issue during the course of this aspect of the examination was the existence of an operation of volunteer or paramilitary groups in Sarajevo and the extent of such involvement. I don't need to go into detail about Mr. Krajisnik's position on that because I'm sure the Court recalls that. But a document which provides information about the existence of such groups, the public praise and acknowledgment that they received and doesn't go beyond that, is surely directly relevant to the question of the accused's knowledge of whether or not such groups were operating, the range of their operations, and the notoriety of such operations. The weight the Court wants to give it, depending on the extent it was emphasised during the cross-examination, may be another matter. But it's clearly relevant and probative and appropriate, in my judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the matter has been discussed so that no new things came up and that the Chamber can decide on the basis of the submissions, the oral submissions, until now, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then decide on the matter and -- but first have a closer look again at the document and the testimony of the witness in relation to it. Anything else on page 8? Then we go to the next page starting at P1229. There's no B/C/S translation for P1229. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, same issue. We'll see that it's resolved as soon as possible. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have a feeling there is one in existence because this is a document that I am objecting to, and I examined the transcript last week in relation to this in some detail. And what happened was at page 25409 to approximately 25411 Mr. Krajisnik was asked about the report and said: "I don't know anything about the report or the bombardment." From recollection, I then objected on the basis that there was no B/C/S translation. One was then found, given to Mr. Krajisnik to read. To be fair to my learned friend, what then happened was there was a break. Immediately after the break a quite lengthy procedural matter was raised. The Chamber might recall, there was the application by the Defence to have the following day off because of Mr. Krajisnik's condition. And cross-examination resumed at page 25418. And my reading of the transcript is nothing more -- was asked about Mr. Krajisnik about this document. So there are two points. First of all, a B/C/S translation was provided to him, and therefore there must be one in existence. I say that to be as helpful as I can. But secondly and more significantly, he wasn't really cross-examined on the document, save for his answer, that he didn't know anything about it. And in those circumstances, notwithstanding the procedural break, in our submission it shouldn't be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my submission Mr. Josse's submissions just now provide the answer to the question of admissibility and to any difficulties arising from the break in proceedings that he described. So further cross-examination on a document that Mr. Krajisnik purports to know nothing about seemingly would have served no purpose; secondly, the answer to the admissibility and relevance and probative value of this document lies precisely in what Mr. Josse just said that Mr. Krajisnik claims to know nothing about a bombardment, which was the subject of contemporaneous discussion which is reflected in this document, with a number of figures, including political leaders outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It clearly has value in the context of that cross-examination and is an appropriate document for impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My only observation is that that is a classic example of the Prosecution continually adding to its case. And my learned friend's submission illustrates that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was a little breath-taking to the Prosecution that Mr. Krajisnik would stand up in open court and say he knew nothing about the shelling of Sarajevo. There's no way, given the submissions by the Defence, the pre-trial brief, and I don't certainly blame my learned friends in this case for that. They weren't here for the original submission of the pre-trial brief, but this is an issue that arose squarely during the course of the Defence case. It's a completely appropriate response by the Prosecution to the position taken by the accused and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter and will give a decision on it. Then the next items on the list are P1230A and P1230B. The registry informs me that it has no possession of these video clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They are available, I'm informed, and we will give them to the registrar today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll now proceed on the basis of the assumption that the registrar will have this material in its possession. Anything else on page 9, Mr. Josse, P1231 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 32, 33. Nothing else. 36 then we move to the next page, page 1234, up to and including P1240. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1241 up to and including P1247?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, so far as P1243 is concerned --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, but I can be of assistance there before Mr. Josse continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1243 is P529, tab 299, already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's helpful. And I therefore have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything else on this page, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: P1244, that was put to Mr. Krajisnik in small part at page 25735. In our submission, only a small part was put to him. He had no knowledge of the document. He was asked to interpret a small part of it and couldn't assist. And this again is an exercise in further supply of evidence by the Prosecution rather than proper cross-examination, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I couldn't disagree more, Your Honour. First of all, it's a very small document, so there's not much in the way of the document -- I mean, of the document to be put to the accused the most relevant part of the document, insofar as I recall, was put to him. I emphasise again it's a quite short document. Secondly, this is not an attempt by the Prosecution to bolster its case through some circumvention of or through some opportunity presented by cross-examination. It's a direct response to what Mr. Krajisnik put during the course of his case, and that is that he knew nothing about the camp system, that the only camp that he later learned about was a secret camp. And during the course of the Prosecution's cross-examination of the position put by Mr. Krajisnik, we put to him that detention facilities for both alleged prisoners of war and civilians had existed from the outset, that an exchange commission was created early on for the purpose of ensuring that those civilian detainees were removed from the territory of Republika Srpska to the other side, that the increasing conquests and military successes of the VRS led to the round-up of many more prisoners, and that those military successes led to the need for the creation of more camps, and that that system was widespread and pervasive enough that all -- that the top leadership of Republika Srpska would have known about that. This was a document reflecting the creation of the Batkovic camp because of the increasing need for additional facilities as a result of the Bosnian Serb military success. The fact that Mr. Krajisnik claims to have no knowledge of it is a factor the Court will have to take into account and weigh against all of the evidence presented by the Prosecution. But in the context of the defence raised by Mr. Krajisnik, this was and remains a perfectly appropriate impeaching document to confront him with in the face of the positions he took during his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the speech the Chamber has just heard sounds like an attempt at bolstering to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was wondering whether we were already final argument, but -- no, no, of course I'm not -- but perhaps, Mr. Tieger, just small reference to its relevance for this and this and this reason would certainly have done, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry for having slightly overpassionate on that, Your Honour, but it just seemed to me that -- well, I had to start from scratch because I felt that the document was -- its relevance was sufficiently obvious that if it wasn't I needed to start from the beginning and place it in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's as far as 1244 is concerned, the Chamber will consider the matter and we'll give a decision. Anything else on this page, P1245 up to 47 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever I am mentioning numbers, that would also include the .1 versions and A and B versions as we find them on the list. P1248 up to and including P1255.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next page, page 13, P1256 and P1257. P1258 and 59. That's the photographic evidence and the CD earlier today. They have been admitted into evidence. Then the two remaining items P1260 and P1261, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, 1261 I discussed with my learned friend. I had submitted that a number of -- much of this interview was highly prejudicial and I think he has agreed that only those parts or that part that was put to Mr. Krajisnik should be admitted into evidence. That's certainly our submission. I understand the Prosecution are agreeable to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then do we receive the -- just a portion of the interview or how are we going to know exactly what is and what is not in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that from the -- I mean, we can do -- there are a couple of expedients. I don't think it's necessary to engage in any formalistic redactions. There was only one portion to the best of my recollection specifically referred to during the examination, and that, I believe, is the portion we agree should be admitted and the rest of it should be disregarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then the decision would be that this will be admitted into evidence, but limited to the specific portion dealt with during the examination of the witness. Another way of -- another way of doing it is that if Mr. Registrar would make available this document to you and you just put on it the relevant portions, then there could be no dispute whatsoever what is evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a practical way of dealing with it. Then -- perhaps I should have taken a different course, but the Defence exhibits were not -- the Prosecution exhibits were first on my list. I therefore now give as a decision of the Chamber that Prosecution Exhibits P1180 up to and including P1261 are admitted into evidence with the following exceptions: P1197 is not yet admitted, still waiting for a limited or reduced version of that document; P1212 was already admitted, therefore does not fall within the scope of this decision; P1221 and P1222 are still pending, due to the fact that there's no B/C/S translation yet; P1226 is still pending and not yet admitted; P1229 is waiting for a translation, and therefore not yet admitted; P1230 -- and P1230A and P1230B are admitted into evidence, but the video is -- clip still to be provided today. Then we have P1243 is not admitted because it was already in evidence and the number is therefore vacated. P1258 and -- now, let me just see. P1244 is still pending and will be decided later. P1258 and 59 were already admitted into evidence earlier today. And P1261 is admitted into evidence, but limited to the portion indicated on the document. That's as far as the exhibits are concerned. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, Your Honour. The Court mentioned that P1229 was still awaiting translation and that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that's the one where --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But the Defence also raised an issue with respect to -- they raised an issue of it independent of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not -- it's not -- that was only one of the issues. But it's still pending and we'll consider it in view of all the submissions we received on the matter. Now we go to the Defence exhibits. That's sometimes a bit more complicated, especially since some of the material which was provided by Mr. Krajisnik have been -- has been given numbers, whereas -- just provisional numbers. And it might well be that we have to further discuss how to deal with those documents, since they were not adopted by either of the parties and since the Chamber has not, of course, received the full index, at least not in an English translation and therefore could not finally make up its mind whether the Chamber itself would like to have some of these documents in evidence. But let's start at the beginning. D183 -- I'm now going first page, starting at D180 -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I think D177 is the first document that was admitted through Mr. Krajisnik, and it was the video clip of the Club 91 interview that was played in part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that you are right that -- that that's the first document, although a decision was given on it on the 6th of June where --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do beg your pardon. I see that now. That applies to 177, 178, and 179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to all three of them. So as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They're already in evidence. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we start now or continue at D180. The first page is D180 up till and including D186. I make the following observations. D183 was admitted already by oral decision of the 6th of June, so is therefore not pending at this moment, and the same is true for D186. Then for D184, we have no English translation yet I think. That's what I find on my list, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see that, too. I fear that the best I can do is ask for the ten days that have been granted in relation to other Defence translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ten days are granted. Then I find on the list that D185, that something would be missing, that it's not in the hands of the registry. But I do understand that it is -- Mr. Haider, is that correct? D185, a transcript of a conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik and Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I'd rather do all these page by page and give decisions because it becomes more complicated at a later stage. So the first page D180 up to and including D185 are admitted into evidence, with the exception of D183, which was admitted into evidence already, and with the exception of D184, due to the lack of an English translation. And the last item on this page D186 was already in evidence. But I've forgotten to ask whether there were any objections, but usually Mr. Tieger ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Only with -- of course -- no, not with respect to anything other than the document for which we have not yet received a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then on the next page. Page 2 goes from D187 up to and including D191. I make the observation that D90 -- D190 and D191 are already admitted, oral decision of the 6th of June. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D187 up to and including D189 are admitted into evidence. On the next page, the -- D192B, D192C, D192D, D192E, and D192F are already admitted into evidence, oral decision of the 6th of June, which leaves two items, that's D193 and D194, both lacking English translations. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it the Court is only asking about D193 and 194.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's the same position. I certainly don't have any independent objection, beyond the fact that I don't -- haven't seen precisely what that document's about in the absence of a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, ten days you would like?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten days are granted. We are now on page 4. The first two items, that is D195 and D196 are already admitted into evidence, oral decision of the 6th of June, so we don't have to deal with them anymore. And now we come to a series, a series D197 up to D217, the letter included. Yes. Here we have -- these are documents that were provided by Mr. Krajisnik and from -- they have not been adopted specifically or -- yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I see they bear my name. From recollection, I was on my feet when they were examined in, albeit, Your Honour, and I mean this fully, Your Honour helped me greatly in that regard. We had all of these translated. There's no difficulty so far as the Defence are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can do one of two things. I can either note the time and try to struggle through these documents during the break, but I, perhaps more accurately, should note that these are documents which the Prosecution would ask for a little additional time to consider. We have not looked through this list -- in particular these documents. And we would like some opportunity to at least refresh our recollection of the context in which they arose and the purpose for which they seem to be introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And my question is then whether the same would be true for D224 through D235, which is the similar series.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well -- yes. Could I make this observation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Clearly the Chamber are trying to deal with this in as pragmatic a way as possible, and I'm not seeking to be critical here, but I -- if there is going to be objection to any of these, I -- the Defence really would ask for advance notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I had the courtesy to sit down with my learned friend and tell him in some detail what my objections were to his documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would ask for the same, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we would be more than pleased to do precisely that, and we did appreciate the opportunity to meet with the Defence. So we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it we have a similar series. We have D224 to D235. We have D238 and D200 -- up till D248. We have D250 to D252. These are all documents that are provided by Mr. Krajisnik himself. If perhaps the parties would discuss whether there are any objections, apart from any technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I would do is speak briefly to Mr. Stewart at -- in relation to whether the Defence -- the Defence counsel adopt these, so to speak. I'm bound to say, Your Honour, I was slightly surprised that in relation to any of the documents that have been given numbers, Your Honour suggested the Defence weren't asking for their admission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- no, I think as a matter of fact, I -- when I said they were not adopted, that I already withdrew that or intended to withdraw that right away. It's not been very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Stewart is nodding his head. Could I therefore say that everything that has been given a number we are seeking the admission of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's then clear, and we'll wait first for the parties to sit together and see whether there are any objections. May I then just leave that list for the time being. I note that D231 misses an English translation, that D237 is already admitted, the same is true for D230 -- I should have said D236, that's double pension legislation, is already admitted. The same is true for D237, which is also double pension legislation. We see that for at least some of the documents in the range of D239 and following that English translations are missing. So especially those documents which -- I think I should leave the whole of the list then in the hands of the parties for the time being. That would be up to and including D256. Then -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got a 257.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- then I'm not -- then I'll try to find D257 during the break. Yes, I see that -- yes, that's an interview with Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no English translation of that document yet either, but we'll leave then everything in the hands of the parties at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll hear from you approximately when it -- it might depend a bit on how we proceed. Tomorrow might be a bit too early or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I, yeah, would ask for a little more time than that, Your Honour, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's to see where somewhere this week, later this week, find some time for dealing with these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Happy with that if the Chamber finds the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course -- I'm thinking in terms of where we have a few moments left to us when we are not examining any witnesses. That's -- that's the issue, as a matter of fact, and to set a time now with the risk of having to ask a witness to stay over a weekend or something like that might not be the best thing to do. And therefore, it's a bit vague but we'll deal with the matter later this week. Then on my agenda I've got two more items. We had a late start, so I think we can continue for a couple of minutes. First of all, the -- the statement or the letter, whatever we call it, of Mr. Karadzic. This was received on the 29th of May, and it was -- translation was received on the 15th of June. The Defence indicated that it would neither adopt nor object to it, and the Prosecution opposed. And the Chamber has asked the Defence to take a position as far as the objections of the Prosecution are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Our position hasn't changed, Your Honour. May we say so far as 92 bis is concerned, without it probably being necessary to go into it, although the formal requirements of 92 bis (B) may not have been complied with, the provisions of 92 bis (C) would leave open the possibility of at least argument on the technical procedural position. But, Your Honour, in the circumstances it really doesn't arise because the Prosecution's position is that they object to admission of this item. The Defence's position is: We don't ask for admission, and in the circumstances we suggest there's no -- there's really no possible reason or justification for its being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The reason of course why the Chamber asked, nevertheless the views of the parties on the matter because Mr. Krajisnik seem -- wanted to offer this to the Chamber as a relevant document. The Chamber has often been rather liberal in accepting documents from a witness who brings relevant documents, and the Chamber of course is in a position to say we nevertheless would like -- even though the parties would not adopt it, that the Chamber could consider to admit it into evidence. But before deciding that the Chamber would or would not, we would like to hear specifically from the parties all the technical aspects, including 92 bis, not only on matters of formality, but also on matters of substance before we finally give a decision on whether or not we would admit this document which has been brought to our attention by a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- first of all, Your Honour, Defence would be the last ever to object to our views being sought. So we certainly have no criticism whatever in relation to that. Your Honour, so far as the very last observation of Your Honour is concerned, perhaps we might suggest if the Prosecution renew or reinforce or indicate their objections on that basis, and then the Defence can add what we wish to add in relation to that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is there anything else you would like to -- or Mr. Harmon, anything else you would like to say about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, first, the document itself goes to the acts or conduct of the accused. It would therefore, in our view, be excludable under Rule 92 bis. The -- second of all, the issue of the formalities, of course it doesn't fall within the issue of the formalities of 92 bis, that's conceded by the parties. That leaves only 92 bis (C), which is a statement which may nevertheless be admitted by a person who can no longer, with reasonable diligence, be traced. I submit, Your Honour, that under those circumstances there has to be some indicia of reliability. In this case Mr. Karadzic has been a fugitive from international justice in excess of ten years, and admitting a statement of an international fugitive from justice would be a -- quite a, I think, bizarre precedent. It is not something that we endorse. We think that the rule should, in its totality, apply to circumstances where the statement itself has some reliability. And under these circumstances, it's our position it has none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm in the odd position. I'm simply not arguing for the admission of this statement at all, Your Honour. But then just very, very briefly at risk that it's a tiny bit academic. Your Honour, the question in those circumstances, however offensive the OTP might find it and suggest it is, it's not Mr. Krajisnik who is a fugitive from justice, and if in different circumstances evidence were of relevance and significance to Mr. Krajisnik's case, then he's not responsible for that difficulty. The technical position is -- and so far as indicia, reliability are concerned, we suggest although it's not a hundred per cent crystal clear from the language that ultimately one is talking about reliability, that it is the statement of the person concerned. And then the assessment of its actual reliability and credibility as evidence is really the next stage once it's been admitted. But, Your Honour, all my submissions being made now are really academic because we're not asking for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, because the witness who produced this document may not be in a position to explain all the technicalities. So more or less you're acting almost as amici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope as amicus should be I'm being helpful and being helpful as much as the Court requires from us this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we have the last item on the agenda, that is all other documents presented by Mr. Krajisnik. That is the documents which have not been given a number yet and of which we have not a full view of what is in there, although we know that many of these documents are already in evidence by now. I suggest to the parties that we'll continue working on it because those documents, as far as not adopted by the parties to be introduced into evidence, the Chamber will have a look at whether it considers that it would assist the Chamber in calling those or having those documents in evidence on the request of the Chamber. Before doing so, if we would like to have some of these documents into evidence, we'll inform the parties so that they can make whatever observations they would like to make before a final decision will be taken. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just return briefly to the Defence exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are a little unclear as to whether the Chamber requires B/C/S translations of D217 and D253 which are English-language documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just find them. D217 you said and -- let me first ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, I'm working from a note that Mr. Sladojevic provided me. I remember 217. Your Honour, in fact, has already previously said that a B/C/S version is not necessary. I recall this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I think that the deadline that was given to the Prosecution to request a B/C/S translation has expired without such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore there's no -- there's no need anymore to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- have it translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But my inquiry does apply to 253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think here we had the -- I think, as a matter of fact, this was mainly about handwriting on it and small changes on the document, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, that's not my recollection. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Elements of agreed principles, and one of the working versions of the Cutileiro --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, the Dayton --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it was Dayton, Sarajevo; I do now remember. If the -- I take it that the OTP is not that much interested in having a B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik indicated in evidence that he at one point had it in his own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, if the Defence -- the original is English -- but if of course a B/C/S copy would be available, then of course we -- not only working for the parties, but also this is a public trial and therefore I'm always a bit hesitant to say we don't need something. Although, of course, if an accused would understand English then many of the documents would not need translation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll ask Mr. Krajisnik when I next speak to him if he has his own --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at this moment it's not therefore required.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, the final matter is D254. I had suggested in an e-mail to a Legal Officer a way to proceed in relation to this. And, very sensibly, the Legal Officer suggested that I should liaise with the Prosecution about my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No doubt they'll consider that and I'd invite them to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the video of the interview with General MacKenzie.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As to whether in fact a full English-language transcript of this is really necessary and justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought it was now included in the list of -- the list you would discuss anyhow with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if it would come up, and translation issues are to be raised, we would hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing at this moment. Then we will adjourn until tomorrow -- Mr. Registrar, I think it's in the morning, 9.00, same courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.50 a.m.,
